name: Judge
label: Revelation
lede: A drummer who was tired of preaching peace wrote the angriest straight edge songs in New York, recorded the album twice, and then spent twenty years away from the monster he'd built.

eras.title: Lyrics from a Florida junkyard
eras.text: Mike Ferraro was drumming for Youth of Today and chafing at its non-violent message. He wrote his own songs on the road, quit, named the new band Judge a week later, and asked John "Porcell" Porcelly to help him make it the most militant straight edge band anyone could imagine.

years.h: Mike Ferraro quits Youth of Today to start Judge
years.p: Parked in a Florida junkyard on a Youth of Today tour, drummer Mike Ferraro fills a notebook with lyrics. Back in New York he tells [[Ray Cappo|e8357f9d-f7f5-4858-a766-aef004bb38a6]] he's leaving, and comes up with the name Judge a week later.

years.h: Mike Ferraro and Porcell make Judge a two-man band
years.p: Mike Ferraro is sharing a Brooklyn apartment with John "Porcell" Porcelly, Al Brown and Ray Cappo. Porcell pushes him to turn his Judge songs into a real band, and signs on to play guitar and bass.

q: I was doing everything to get that reaction.
years.src: Vice: Behind the Quiet, Part II · Wikipedia
years.h: New York Crew 7", Judge's debut · Schism Records
years.p: John "Porcell" Porcelly on guitar and bass, Mike Ferraro singing and drumming. Five songs, including a cover of Blitz's Warriors, out on Schism, the label Porcell ran with Alex Brown.
years.xp:
Porcell objected that some of Mike Ferraro's first lyrics read like confessions to crimes, and Ferraro rewrote an ending. Even so, a reference to Boston on New York Crew was taken as a direct challenge by the Boston crew around the band Choke.

Ferraro says he was chasing exactly that reaction, and was still shocked when it came.

years.h: Judge's first show, at the Anthrax in Connecticut
years.p: To play live, Mike Ferraro and Porcell bring in drummer [[Drew Thomas|ebc66701-0d59-49c9-ae21-4937edb96a6a]] from [[Bold|b024b1bd-2020-4b7c-83f7-4660133c89fa]] and Jimmy Yu on bass. Yu and drummer [[Luke Abbey|6ab9b327-0f98-4515-907c-13078f426cc5]] become Judge's 1988–89 rhythm section.

eras.title: So good they recorded it twice
eras.text: Judge's first album cost real money at Chung King in Manhattan, and the band hated it. They started over in Rhode Island, and Revelation quietly pressed the rejected version for the fans who'd already paid.

years.big: 110 copies of the album they threw away
years.src: Revelation Records pressing history · Wikipedia: Bringin' It Down
years.h: Revelation presses Judge's rejected Chung King album anyway
years.p: In January 1989 Judge recorded their first album at Chung King in Manhattan, ran up a real bill, and rejected it. To cover preorders, Revelation pressed it on white vinyl as Chung King Can Suck It.
years.xp:
The session had Mike Ferraro and Porcell with [[Sammy Siegler|869c662b-574c-46ac-acf6-3dc6f025fd5a]] on drums and Matt Pincus on bass; two of its songs never made Bringin' It Down. Revelation planned 100 copies, but the plant made 110, and the extra ten had the first zero in the hand-numbered /100 written over with a 1.

Jordan Cooper and Porcell both believed only three test pressings existed; Porcell sold one thinking it was a Bringin' It Down test. Copies now sell for over a thousand dollars, and according to Wikipedia one went for $6,600 on eBay. Revelation has said it never made money on them.

years.h: Bringin' It Down, Judge's album · Revelation REV 15
years.p: Judge's re-recorded album, made at Normandy Sound in Rhode Island and produced by Porcell and Tom Soares. Revelation's tag line: so good they had to record it twice.
years.xp: Normandy Sound is where the [[Cro-Mags|9ffa627f-32c2-4cb1-bfad-00cf348abc70]] cut Best Wishes. Nine songs in 22 minutes.

years.h: Revelation reissues Judge's New York Crew as REV 14
years.p: Revelation re-presses Judge's debut 7": 4,000 on black vinyl and 1,000 on blue, in an orange sleeve.

eras.title: The kids took it literally
eras.text: Judge had set out to provoke, and the provocation worked too well. The last record, There Will Be Quiet..., got darker and more reflective, while the shows filled with fights and worse, and Mike Ferraro decided he couldn't stop what he'd started.

years.h: There Will Be Quiet..., Judge's last record · REV 20
years.p: [[Lars Weiss|c60d8790-7786-4df8-8647-7f8b2ca02c17]] joins on guitar. The Storm and Forget This Time show a slower, bleaker Judge; the CD adds a cover of [[Led Zeppelin|678d88b2-87b0-403b-b63d-5da7465aecc3]]'s When the Levee Breaks.

years.h: Ex-Judge bassist Jimmy Yu becomes a Buddhist monk
years.p: Jimmy Yu, Judge's bassist in 1988–89, is ordained a Chan Buddhist monk under Master Sheng Yen, taking the name Guogu. He goes on to a Princeton PhD in 2008 and a job teaching religion at Florida State University.

q: Every word I ever wrote was thrown back into my face.
years.h: Violence at a Tampa show, and Judge ends
years.p: At a Tampa show on Judge's last tour, the Village Voice reported, white power chants start early and a group attacks a Black man in the crowd. Mike Ferraro confronts it from the stage, and Judge ends that year.
years.xp:
From the stage Mike Ferraro asked what six guys on one older man proved, and asked the room to get through the last song in peace. It was a pattern, not one night: at another stop someone called the house Judge were staying in and asked Ferraro to go beat up members of the KKK holding a rally in town.

Maximum Rock'N'Roll had long criticized Judge's militant edge, and Ferraro later admitted provocation was the point. He told the Voice he felt responsible, big-time, that kids were fighting while singing his lyrics at him, and that he couldn't stop what he'd put in motion. So he left.

eras.title: Ferraro goes quiet, the records don't
eras.text: Mike Ferraro left the scene almost completely. Judge's recordings kept circulating, officially and as bootlegs, until Revelation gathered everything onto one disc, What It Meant, in 2005.

years.h: Bootlegs of Judge's Chung King session get out
years.p: Bootlegs, not Revelation releases: No Apologies: The Chung King Sessions and Revelation Can Suck It put Judge's rejected session back in circulation, alongside a live WNYU broadcast, Vivo En WNYU.

years.h: Mike Ferraro's next act: Mike Judge and Old Smoke
years.p: Mike Ferraro's Neil Young-leaning acoustic project with former Judge roadie Todd Schwartz releases the Sights 12" on Revelation. Then Ferraro mostly disappears from music.

years.h: What We Said... And Where It Went: a Judge retrospective
years.p: The first Judge retrospective comes out while the band stays dormant.

years.h: What It Meant: The Complete Discography
years.p: Revelation puts all of Judge's recordings in one place, sixteen years after Bringin' It Down.

eras.title: Twenty years, then Webster Hall
eras.text: An appearance on East Village Radio drew Mike Ferraro back out after roughly two decades away. The reunion that followed was two nights at Webster Hall in New York, then the world, and a documentary that told the story in the band's own words.

years.h: Mike Ferraro back on the air
years.p: Mike Ferraro turns up on Black N' Blue Takeover on East Village Radio, the appearance that starts Judge's road back.

years.h: Judge reunite for two nights at Webster Hall
years.p: Mike Ferraro, Porcell, Sammy Siegler and Matt Pincus, with [[Charlie Garriga|4f24f7e7-bc37-45d1-8f60-99bc992cd780]] on second guitar, play New York's Webster Hall. Tours of the US, South America and Europe follow through 2014 and 2015.

years.h: There Will Be Quiet: The Story of Judge (Noisey documentary)
yt: There Will Be Quiet: The Story of Judge (Noisey documentary)

years.h: There Will Be Quiet: The Story of Judge
years.p: A roughly hour-long documentary in four parts, directed by Seth Lowery and Judge drummer Sammy Siegler, premieres through the Village Voice and Noisey.

eras.title: Night one in Los Angeles
eras.text: Judge stayed a working reunion band, the heavy end of the Revelation family on its big bills, with Porcell and Sammy Siegler still behind Mike Ferraro.

years.h: Judge play The Book of Revelation Records, Los Angeles
years.p: Judge co-headline night one of the two-night Book of Revelation Records shows at the 1720 in Los Angeles, with 7 Seconds. Youth of Today and [[Side By Side|8dc812b1-d387-4c45-8173-f0d5bd0c318f]] take night two.

years.h: Mike Ferraro raises chickens in West Virginia
years.p: Between shows, Judge singer Mike Ferraro lives quietly: according to Wikipedia, he raises chickens on a family farm in West Virginia.
